newsitem.title: GREECE: Sea of apathy sweeps Greece's election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Sea of apathy sweeps Greece's election campaign.

text.p: The usually bustling political party offices in this Western Greek town are quiet and nearly empty, reflecting the nation's widespread indifference to Sunday's close election.

"When I was on the campaign trail, I was followed by 100 cars honking their horns through villages," former socialist deputy Christos Bassayannis told Reuters. "Now the official line from Athens is to tone it down."
Across from the crowded cafes of the main square are the deserted conservative party offices.

"Long gone and forgotten..." goes the song blaring from the television. It seems a nostalgic anthem to traditional campaigning, with larger-than-life politicians spouting fiery speeches in front of huge chanting crowds in squares all over Greece.
"Times have changed. Young people have other interests now," says a conservative opposition campaign official, Dimitris Haidemenos. "We have orders not to pollute and not to paint slogans."

Gone are the trademarks of past elections -- the socialist green, conservative blue and communist red slogans painted alongside country roads, and the vans pasted with candidates' posters criss-crossing towns and blasting party songs.

The dramatic change in style comes just three months after the death of flamboyant socialist leader and premier Andreas Papandreou, who would draw thousands of near-fanatical supporters to his boisterous rallies.

Both his demure successor, Prime Minister Costas Simitis, and stocky, outspoken challenger Miltiadis Evert have spurned the old ways and have campaigned mostly on television, prompting the press to dub this the "couch election".
Opinion polls show a public unimpressed with both candidates and issues, and seemingly turning to smaller parties, sending shock waves through the corridors of power in Athens.
Simitis, who relies heavily on the provincial vote, has admitted he might have miscalculated the Greeks' need to touch their politicians and has belatedly hit the campaign trail.

"We realised that often people need to be mobilised in order to participate," he said in an interview this week. Towns like picturesque Messolongi, where the English poet Lord Byron died in 1824, are the socialists' main strength.
About 10,000 residents living mainly off the fish farms of its vast lagoon elected five socialist and only two conservative deputies in the last election.
"There are many who are nostalgic for the old style," former deputy Bassayannis said. "The government wanted this European style of elections. We will see how effective it will be."

Analysts say, however, that the new style may be inevitable, reflecting not so much a choice by politicians as their lacklustre personalities and lack of real policy differences in light of strict European Union requirements for Greece.

"Parties have come so close to converging on issues that it is difficult to pin huge rallies on their differences," a western diplomat in Athens said. "When Brussels makes the rules, it requires conservative campaigning."
